At the request of the various dharma-heirs of Shouchang, the Master ascended the hall. Looking to his left and right, he said:
"The elders have all risen; ha ha ha! They have lost five cents and a half. How often has one next door ever set out an abacus? There is no silver thirty taels here;
what harm is there in playing at being a fool for a thousand ages? This is not to be taken lightly—do not speak of it easily. The world is full [of such things]."

In one’s youth, there was the story of boring through a wall to steal light; borrowing a shadow to pass through a pass. What does this have to do with having a tally or a seal from a provincial governor?
Only those among us who take the Dharma as their kin can, like Yang Xiu upon seeing the "Young Lady" inscription, find themselves unable to contain their joy.
[The Master] descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, the Master remained silent for a long while and said, "Do you understand? The events of ten thousand ages cannot equal me.
A single flicker of my eyebrows cannot equal me. A single dot on my forehead cannot equal me.
A single strike of my staff cannot equal me. He let out a thunderous shout. "If you do not understand, let the lanterns and the pillars take your place."
"You go down to the Nirvana Hall. Now tell me, why is it so? Alas! A man dead on the spot—what means of salvation is there?
He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, the Master called out, "Assembly! At this very moment, who is not with their entire being fully contained within it?
He then extended his hand and said, "Why is it that your lives are in my hands? The assembly had no reply.
The Master spoke again, "Why is it that the life of Śākyamuni is at the soles of your feet? Again, the assembly was at a loss.
"Chuò! The Master then clapped his hands and said: "The breeze is warm and the birds' songs shatter; the sun is high and the flower shadows deepen.

Having concluded the retreat and taken leave of the assembly, he ascended the hall. Gazing alone from a solitary pavilion, the spring mountains stretch afar; the nine bends flow clear and pure day and night.
How joyful that this splendor flows on without end—by the willow-lined embankment, the moon has just risen. "Great Assembly! One binding."
One interpretation: This is originally the standard of conduct for all time. Whether in stillness or in action, the karmic conditions must have their own source.
Today, this mountain monk addresses the assembly to entrust the staff; it wishes to depart toward the peaks of ten thousand mountains.
The great assembly repeatedly entreated him to remain so that the Dharma might endure for a long time. The Master said: "The assembly, speak from the tip of my staff."
When the assembly approached, the Master remained seated. As they hesitated, he struck the ground once with his staff and said, "From the beginning we have lived together, yet no one recognizes it;
let out a long cry and go back. He then descended from his seat.
Small Sermon: To cross the silken threads of the nine bends, a swift steed is no match for a tiny ant; to gather the nectar of the myriad flowers, a phoenix is no equal to a humble bee.
For this reason, the sages were able to employ each person according to their talent, thereby fulfilling the creative virtue of the Maker.
You must know that there is yet a further, upward-moving pivot. It is just as Qianfeng said: "Lift it up!"
"One must not raise two; if you let one point pass, you fall into the second. What is the underlying meaning? Have you not seen Yunmen say:
"Yesterday someone came from Tiantai; today he is going to Jingshan"?
If you understand it here, then tomorrow the head cook will not have to go on the communal labor duty. It is exactly like a box and its lid fitting together. If...
This will not do. Even if you were to cut off all streams of thought, the Southern Dipper remains seven and the Northern Dipper remains eight.
A wooden horse spurred on stretches out its two legs; an iron ox pierced by a tethering rope bows its head low. *Chan*.
A Small Sermon. An ancient said: "If one descends from heaven, one is poor; if one wells up from the earth, one is wealthy and noble.

That which is wealthy and noble is not worth a single coin, while that which is poor cannot be exchanged for ten thousand pieces of gold. Throughout my life, this mountain monk has been nothing but bare bone and skin.
I have never seen anyone descend from heaven or spring up from the earth; there is only a pair of empty hands.
Whether they be rich or poor, as soon as they arrive, I give them a slap. Why? Because my rewards and punishments are clear and distinct, all affairs naturally come to rest.
At Huixin Garden, the Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Who has ever realized the mind? He struck his left side with his hand and said, "What a pity!
He then asked again, "And how would you realize the mind? He struck his right side with his hand and said: [The Master then descended from his seat.]
"What a pity! he said. Then he added, "Now that this mountain monk has arrived here, how will you all converse with me?
He then raised his fist and said, "What a pity! Layman Zhang asked, "What a fine 'what a pity'! But alas, those who truly understand are few.
The Master said, "The moon rises over a thousand peaks; it is dark and yet bright. Layman Zhang said, "It pierces right through people's nostrils."
The Master said, "How could you have brought this upon yourself? The Layman said, "Let us let the Great Master off this time.
The Master said, "This mountain monk is at fault. The Layman bowed and said, "Will you grant me the intimate words from the peak of Huanglong?
The Master said, "The Layman is merely divining with a ladle and listening for an empty sound. The Layman said, "The Great Master has gone off in that way again. The Master said, "Why?"
Thus, he grasped his topknot and went to the yamen. The scholar said, "Your fangs and claws are too prominent. The Master said, "Lower your head and look at the stars.
The scholar bowed.
At Jingguantang, he addressed the assembly. Huang Xiaolian of Wenling asked, "Has the Great Master ever crossed the Luoyang Bridge?"
"Not yet," the Master said. "Look at the tip of the staff. Lián said, "In that case, you are a master who is well-versed in handling this serpent.
The Master said, "You must also remain on guard against him. The scholar said, "This is where a great spiritual friend does not let anything pass."
"It is precisely compassion. The Master said, "There is no need to calculate it down to the ounce or the tael. The Master then said, "On the bridge at Luoyang, there is a great deal of elegance;
who can handle the tip of the staff with such ease? One must enter where there is nothing to guard against;
one must strictly avoid calculating ounces and taels. Within this, there is something extraordinary. It is left to the bystander with eyes to perceive it. As for Keju..."
A gentleman who had visited me in the interim asked about the *gong'an* of the Elder Daguan regarding the circle. Is there anyone who can judge it?
I, this mountain monk, shall once again offer a turning word for it: "Precisely because it is so utterly clear, it causes what is attained to be delayed."
Huanghua addressed the assembly. He cited the case of Han Yu, the Duke of Wen, who, upon hearing the words of Sanping, attained a point of entry.
The Master said: "The Duke of Wen was in a cauldron of boiling water where there was no place for cold; he sought a single ladle of coolness.
Dadian [Dajian] thrust his body into a forest of sword-trees to open a single thread of the living path. Sanping, however, carved a tiger onto the door plaque to startle him."
Foolish people! Furthermore, when Duke Wen was playing with a ball on a rapid current, it rolled away every time.
If one can truly see through the point where birth and death intersect with a single glance, I allow that such a person may walk hand-in-hand with me;
otherwise, you are like a blind donkey following the crowd, merely falling into pits and ravines yourself. Tell me, what is this "point where birth and death intersect"?
He pierced [the truth] with a single glance. He snapped his fingers once and said, "I reckon there is no connection.
On the anniversary of the passing of the late Master Shouchang, the Teacher addressed the assembly, saying:

"You should know that this old man had nothing particularly extraordinary during his lifetime. He merely possessed four kinds of antiquities by which his fame spread throughout the world. Yet, alas, now they have fallen into..."
In the hands of a nobleman, it might be used to polish a square bamboo staff, turn an old bronze bottle, or paint with gold, ink, and water;
it might even be used to lacquer a broken-stringed zither with colorful ornamentation. If people of the age were to see it, they would surely find it exquisite.
However, one must not let a true master see it. What happens when a master sees it? *Ai!* [Sigh]—and he immediately returned to his quarters.

[The Master] picks up and comments on a verse praising the World-Honored One at his birth: with one hand pointing to heaven and the other pointing to earth, he walked seven steps and looked around in the four directions, letting out a lion’s roar and saying, "In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored. Later, Yunmen said, "I [should have said...]"
"If at that time you see [him], strike him dead with a single blow and give him to the dogs to eat, so as to ensure peace throughout the world.
He then held up his staff and said: "Is it truly so? If one does not find strange what is strange, the strangeness will naturally vanish.
It is laughable that even in later generations there are still those who try to drive a stake into empty space."
The verse says: The world is without beginning, yet it has a beginning; Holding the staff askew, he stands alone in contemplation.
To point this out clearly is already a great deal of fuss; Throughout the ages, who would not find this naturally satisfying?
The World-Honored One practiced austerities for six years on Mount Snowy; then, on the eighth night of the twelfth lunar month, upon seeing the morning star, he attained great enlightenment.
[The Master] took up the case and said: "When he was first born, his eyes gazed in the four directions—this would have made him blind. Were it not so, how could he have reached this night?"
At first one sees the stars; even if you see them with such clarity and distinctness, that is precisely where you are blind.
The verse says: "Not resting his feet upon the Dragon Throne, He gazes at the heavens on a snowy peak at night.
Who knows the hand that shifts the Dipper and moves the stars? It has deceived the eyes of all, past and present, leaving them incomplete."
The World-Honored One once held up a flower at the assembly on Vulture Peak; the multitude were all at a loss, yet only Kāśyapa broke into a smile.
The World-Honored One said: "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*, the Dharma-gate of the signless true reality."
"I entrust this to you.
[The Master] held up the whisk and said: "Great or small, the World-Honored One has experienced many things; how could he not know that 'the sharp tools of the world must not be shown to others'?
And yet, he was not good at concealing their use."
The verse says: I have ground my sword throughout my life, never daring to treat it lightly; Only at year’s end do I encounter a single hero.
Having cast it off, what use could it possibly have? From this point on, the world shall not be at peace.
When the World-Honored One’s assembly had concluded and everyone had dispersed, a single woman remained close to the Buddha’s seat. Mañjuśrī did not realize this and asked the Buddha about her.
The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to emerge from his samādhi and question her himself; however, Mañjuśrī exhausted all his supernatural powers and was unable to rouse him.
The Buddha said, "Below, there is the Great Being Vimalakīrti who can bring him out. In a moment, Vimalakīrti arrived. With a single...
He snapped his fingers. The woman immediately emerged from meditative absorption.
[The Master] remarked: "This group of fellows is much like those who, having no business at all, nevertheless each try to show off their own wares."
This is a method for dispelling [delusions]. Alas! There is a thorn within the mire.

If I were to see a woman emerging from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), I would immediately ask her, "What kind of concentration did you enter? While she was about to respond, I would let out a shout and say, "You wild fox spirit!
Why are you still making such a fuss here? Only when she is made to urinate on the spot will she find relief.
The verse says: The weather that tires the spirit is half-sunny, half-shaded; Outside the window, yellow orioles send forth their fine songs.
Having awakened from sleep, I have no leisure for matters of grooming; Instead, beneath the flowers, I wipe my jade zither.
To cite the Great Being Bodhidharma’s coming from the West: he sat facing a wall at Shaolin on Mount Song for nine years. On six occasions he ingested poison but did not die;
he encountered Shen Guang, who stood in the snow and severed his own arm to seek the Dharma. The Master took pity on him and thus named him Huik’e.
Huik’e asked, “My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace of mind. The Master said, “Bring forth your mind, and I shall pacify it for you.”
Huineng said, "You may say: 'I have sought the mind, but it is ultimately unattainable. Huineng replied, "I have finished settling your mind for you.
After some time, the Master knew that the conditions were ripe; he then commanded his disciples to each speak of what they had attained.
Only Huineng, at the very end, performed three prostrations and stood in his place. The Master said, "You have attained my marrow."
The Master held up his staff and said: "Coming from the West and sitting facing a wall—this was enough to leave people in doubt.
Yet, that final act of dividing the skin and dividing the marrow—what a total failure! And who could possibly save it?"
The verse says: Last night I ascended the western tower alone; I was glad that the new autumn moon was so profound.
I tried blowing a single melody on my jade flute; How much sorrow it stirred in the hearts of travelers!
[The Master] raised the case of Qingyuan seeing the Sixth Patriarch. [Qingyuan] asked, "What should one attend to so as not to fall into stages?
The Patriarch said, "What have you been doing? He replied, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths. The Patriarch said, "In what stage would you then fall?
He replied, "If I do not even practice the Noble Truths, what stages could there be? The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. Guard and maintain this well for yourself."
The Master picks up the case and says: "One has a presence like a king; the other has cut off heaven and earth.

There is no avoiding it—taking the hand to climb the high mountain, one's heels are seen through by another in a single glance. Had I been the Sixth Patriarch, when he asked, 'What should one’s primary concern be?
I would not have fallen into the trap of hierarchical stages. I would have immediately shouted: 'You dung-carrier! Be here! "
"What would you do? If one were Qingyuan, upon hearing the Sixth Patriarch ask, "What have you been doing?
he would have clapped his hands and said, "This old fellow is still talking in his sleep! Would this not cause the path of Caoxi to possess a distinct splendor?
The verse says: "Self-pitying, illumination exhausted, the essence has no support; Turning toward Caoxi, I speak of the Patriarch’s pivot. Facing each other in clarity...
The wind brushes against the white moon; flowers fall before the courtyard, carried away by birds.
Mazu raised up Qingyuan’s instruction for Shitou to deliver a letter to Nanyue. Upon arriving at Nanyue, Shitou immediately asked:
"When one does not admire the various sages and does not prize one's own spiritual essence, what then? Nanyue said: "Your question is too lofty, my son. Why not ask about things below?"
Tou said, "I would rather fall into the depths of samsara for eternal kalpas than seek liberation through the various sages. With this, he shook out his sleeves and departed.
Qingyuan asked him, "How was your meeting with Master Xiangruo? He replied, "I did not even exchange a letter, nor did I deliver a message.
When I left, I was granted by the Master the promise of a single-edged axe to dwell in the mountains; I request it now. Qingyuan then lowered one of his feet.
He immediately bowed.
[The Master] picked up the staff and said: "A lion teaches its cub; there is another way to cast it aside. As for this adze, where can one rub it?
Yet, both the two elders, Qingyuan and Nanyue, had their moments of letting go. I do not admire the various sages, nor do I value..."

Regarding the line "How is one's own spirit at such a time? [Dongshan] acted on behalf of Nanyue by striking him across the back with a staff and saying, "Do you still have the sound of a hot bowl ringing in your ears?
He thus caused him to pursue a different way of life. Furthermore, regarding the line "The question of the son is too high; why not ask downward?
[Dongshan] acted on behalf of Shitou by letting out a great shout and saying, "You rotten winter melon, old man! Is this fit?
"What is he doing? If it were so, there would be no need to wait for his return; even Qingyuan’s *caofu* (whetstone axe) would no longer show its edge.
The verse says: "Just as he leaves the Dragon Gate, he enters the Tiger’s Den; when a man of spirit reaches this point, he stands tall and majestic of himself. Upon returning, he seizes...
He obtained his father’s axe and cleared away the wilderness along the eastern and western paths.
Once, seeing Mazu sitting in meditation upon a rock before the hermitage at Nanyue, he began grinding a brick against it there.
The Patriarch asked Huairang, "What is the purpose of polishing this tile? Huairang replied, "To make a mirror. The Patriarch said, "How can polishing a tile produce a mirror?
Huairang then asked, "What are you doing here, Venerable Sir? The Patriarch replied, "I am practicing meditation. Huairang said, "What is the point of practicing meditation?"
[The Master] said, "I am attempting to become a Buddha. Huairang said, "Just as my grinding of this brick cannot produce a mirror, how can your sitting in meditation possibly produce a Buddha?
The Master then asked, "What then is the way? Huairang said, "It is like a cart that will not move: you may strike the cart, or you may strike the ox.
He further demonstrated this using the analogy of seeds and the moisture from heaven; when the conditions coincide, one naturally perceives it for oneself.
The Master spoke at length, whereupon the Patriarch attained thorough enlightenment.
He remarked: "A fine steed has already emerged from the stable; it does not matter that the shadow of the whip falls repeatedly.

Yet, compared to the later practice where blows and shouts are hurled in rapid succession, there have already been many who have mastered the Way. Nevertheless, at that time, the Gate of the School was in its initial development."
The great capacity [of the practitioner] is indeed already such as this. Yet, if one single-mindedly pursues only the path of crude and impetuous speed, how could one ever hope to equal the ancients?
The verse says: "The brick has been ground and the cart is already moving; the eye-mind of the colt is naturally brilliant. With a clear boundary, he steps forth."
He killed countless people. It is truly laughable how efficacious that prophecy from the Western Heaven was.
Once, when the meal was late, Deshan took up his alms bowl and headed toward the monks' hall himself.
Seeing this, Xuefeng said, "The bell has not yet rung and the drum has not yet sounded; where is this old fellow going with his bowl? Deshan returned to his quarters without saying a word.
Dazhu raised this matter for Yantou to consider. Yantou said, "Great Master Deshan has not yet realized the final word.
Deshan then instructed his attendant to ask Yantou, "Do you not approve of me, old monk? Yantou secretly conveyed his meaning.
The next day, when Deshan ascended the hall, it was indeed different from his usual self. Yantou stood before the Dharma Hall and clapped his hands, saying, "How joyful!"
The old man understood the final word. Nevertheless, he was destined to live for only three years. Shanguo passed away after three years.
[Xuedou] comments:
"Not all matters in the world are like this; one must carefully observe the point where father and son meet in terms of benefit and harm."
The verse says: The resentment over the plundered nest has long endured; how could its settling have not yet been extinguished? Sacred wisdom has always been a resource for thieves and robbers;
they do not employ talismans and seals as a sound strategy.
Citing Zhaozhou’s encounter with a monk: There was once an old woman at Mount Tai who, whenever asked where the road to Mount Tai led, would say, "Go straight ahead.
As soon as the monk had taken a step, she would say, "This monk is going off again like that."
Zhaozhou said, "I have thoroughly investigated and exposed this old woman for you. Zhaozhou then went to that same place and asked her the same question;
she answered in exactly the same way. Zhaozhou returned and reported it, saying, "I have thoroughly investigated and exposed her for you."

The Master picks up the case and says: "This foul old woman not only outwitted the wandering monks of the world, but there is not a single old fellow sitting on a curved wooden chair in all quarters who has not been outwitted by her as well.
Now tell me, when Zhaozhou said he had 'seen through' her, did he actually manage to get out of this old woman's trap? When meeting people, do not misrepresent [the teaching]."
The verse says: "Traveling through a hundred cities of misty waters, each deeply investigating— How does this compare to the single pointing-out at Mount Tai?
Old Zhao did not hesitate to drive down another stake; Everyone has no place to hide their shame."
Dongshan, having already realized that insentient beings preach the Dharma, wished to take his leave of Yunyan.

He asked, "If someone asks me after I have left here, 'Can you depict the true likeness of the Master? how would you answer him? Yunyan remained silent for a long while and then said, "It is just this."
Shan sighed deeply. Yanguan said, "Reverend Jia, you must be extremely careful in undertaking this matter.
Later, while crossing a stream, Shan saw his reflection and attained great enlightenment regarding the profound principle.
The Master picks up the case and says: "Old man Yunyan has poison in his mouth; to touch it is to lose one's life. Yet, alas, he is far from sharp.
Why did he not wait for Dongshan to ask and then push him out?
Had Dongshan been a truly fierce fellow, seeing that Yunyan remained silent for a long while, he would have overturned the meditation seat, laughed loudly, and walked out. Then, after this..."
He will not go on in such a manner again.
The verse says: Hearing sounds with the eyes already blocks the ford; Touching upon taboos before the pivot further injures the spirit.
The talisman for protecting the body is suddenly cast away; Picking up a tortoise-hair, he kills and brings people to life.
After Yangtai had already entrusted [the lineage] to many people, they all passed away first. Fushan Yuan, who succeeded Yexian, had also long received the Master’s teachings.
Yangtai then gave him his crown-protuberance skin sandals and a verse, charging him to seek out a successor on his behalf to continue this Dongshan school.
Fushan indeed found Touzi Qing, who deeply realized the essential tenets; he immediately [presented him with] Yangtai’s crown-protuberance...
He presented the verse on the leather sandals and composed his own verse: "A Mount Sumeru stands in the vast void; The sun and moon revolve as its attendants.
The myriad peaks gradually lean upon it, While the white clouds undergo their transformations. The wind of Shaolin rises amidst the thickets; The bamboo curtain of Caoxi is rolled up.
The golden phoenix dwells in the dragon’s nest; How could the imperial moss ever be crushed by a carriage wheel? With this, he entrusted him [the verse] to him, making him the successor to Dayang.
The Master holds up the staff and says: "To graft wood and produce flowers is a marvel of the power of the spring within the seed-nature.
At the point where Fushan won both prizes at once, observe the principle of the golden phoenix nesting in the dragon’s lair—how extraordinary and unprecedented it is!"
The verse says: Sending forth and gathering back possess a great capacity; reaching the ultimate ground is most precarious and subtle.
Pushing up Mount Sumeru from within space, the wind rolls back the curtain of Songshan as the mountain peak glows.

[The Master] recounted how Shouchang first visited Lingshan. After he attained a realization while studying the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Lingshan said, "If the eye of the school is not clear, you have not yet reached the ultimate.
Later, while reading the records of a monk who asked Chan Master Weikuan of Xingshan, "What is the Way?
Weikuan replied, "A magnificent mountain. The monk asked, "I am asking about the Way; why do you say 'a magnificent mountain'? Weikuan said, "You only know..."

"How wonderful this great mountain! When have I ever attained the Way? Chang suddenly gave rise to a state of doubt. After eight months had passed, he happened to be moving a stone that he could not lift;
as he exerted all his strength to move it, he was suddenly and greatly enlightened. He said: "If one wishes to study the unsurpassed path of Bodhi, one must urgently clear away this great mountain.
Only when one knows the Way does one realize the mountain is not so great; turning over and leaping out, one passes through the barrier of the Patriarchs. This is...
He presented this to Lingshan. Lingshan re-examined it and granted his seal of approval (*inka*). [Xuedou] comments:

"What is so good about this old fellow? If it were not for this magnificent mountain, I would guarantee that even after as many donkey years as there are hairs on a donkey’s tail, you still would not have dreamed of it."
The verse says: A white snake blocking the road was indeed slain; The red-eyed hero has another plan.
Since departing the tiger’s den at Hongmen, The tyrannical Qin and the powerful Chu have led the way.
The Five Ranks: Right within the Deviant.
Suddenly a thunderclap resounds through the nine heavens; Like a spark from stone or a flash of lightning, it cannot be pursued.
Who can attain sudden awakening before the skull?
From partiality, one enters correctness. Meeting face-to-face, one is not permitted to gaze into the Qin mirror. Solemnly holding hands, one ascends the mountain of blades.
What kind of *nāga* is this that is always in samādhi? Coming from the very center:
the wooden man and stone woman dance the Three Terraces. The ten thousand nations sing praises, forgetting the Emperor’s power. General’s Seal.
The sword cuts through the dust of war;
it reaches the ultimate point. Entering the demon, entering the Buddha—compassion and wisdom are complete. In this era of Great Peace throughout the realm, people remain forever deluded and stubborn.
The iron ox has plowed through the golden earth.

Simultaneously reaching the center. Noble and natural, who dares to speak of it? Continuity from the beginning has always been most difficult; at that very moment, one does not recognize the subtlety of the ancestors. Verses on the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials: The first mystery is like a mirror facing a wall; The second mystery is like a sword hanging in space; The third mystery is like a dragon emerging from the sea. The first essential is like a bird flying through the sky; The second essential is like a fish leaping over the waves; The third essential is like a pearl hidden in the mud. The three mysteries and three essentials are all here; If you can see them clearly, you will not be deluded. If you do not understand this, you are lost in vain; Even if you study for a hundred years, what benefit is there? The first mystery is like a mirror facing a wall— It reflects all things without discrimination.

The second mystery is like a sword hanging in space— Sharp and penetrating, leaving no trace. The third mystery is like a dragon emerging from the sea— Its power and majesty are beyond compare. The first essential is like a bird flying through the sky— Soaring freely without obstruction. The second essential is like a fish leaping over the waves— Swift and unimpeded in its movement. The third essential is like a pearl hidden in the mud— Pure and bright, though obscured by defilement. These three mysteries and three essentials are all present; If you can see them clearly, you will not be deluded. If you do not understand this, you are lost in vain; Even if you study for a hundred years, what benefit is there?
The First Mystery: Who could know that the Eastern Land and the Western Heaven are one? At Shaolin, they vainly divided skin from marrow;
even iron walls and silver mountains must be pierced through.
The Second Mystery: Upon the bare flesh-ball, a sharp point descends with pain. To push away the causeless dry dung-stick—vast and boundless, what is this?
Abiding in the midst of gratitude and resentment—this is the third mystery.
Within the purple silk curtain, it is not lightly transmitted. When the opportunity strikes and one is pressed, there is no place to escape;
captured and defeated, it is found to be originally worthless.

The first essential: The ancient Buddhas could not have focused their minds on it; yet, as they followed along, there was something of it. Moving among the heterodox without leaving a trace—this is the second essential.
Why labor to seek fodder when you are already in your own place? Picking up whatever comes to hand, the power to kill or give life is wondrous. To deliberate upon it is to fail.
When both are lost from view, this is the third essential.
A vermilion dot marks the seal, opening it into a distinct tune. Before the pivot, one falls into a tiger’s trap—how could one allow such a sight?
Only when all thieving minds are extinguished will one truly burst into laughter.

Because a monk asked, "Why did Dongshan establish these five ranks? the Master said, "They are merely pieces of furniture for leisure. The monk pressed further, "How then can they be taken as the fundamental principle? The Master said, "Tell me, who is able to extract the nails and pegs of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? He then presented this verse: The five ranks are like a house; If you enter, you must know the way. If you do not know the way, You will stumble and fall. If you know the way, You will walk with ease. If you do not walk with ease, You will be lost in the weeds. If you walk with ease, You will reach the ultimate. If you reach the ultimate, You will see the source. If you see the source, You will be free from all constraints. If you are free from all constraints, You will be at peace. If you are at peace, You will be in accord with the Way. If you are in accord with the Way, You will be in harmony with all things. If you are in harmony with all things, You will be one with the universe. If you are one with the universe, You will be the Buddha. If you are the Buddha, You will be the Dharma. If you are the Dharma, You will be the Sangha. If you are the Sangha, You will be the Three Jewels. If you are the Three Jewels, You will be the Great Vehicle. If you are the Great Vehicle, You will be the Bodhisattva. If you are the Bodhisattva, You will be the Tathāgata. If you are the Tathāgata, You will be the World-Honored One. If you are the World-Honored One, You will be the Teacher of Gods and Men. If you are the Teacher of Gods and Men, You will be the Savior of All Beings. If you are the Savior of All Beings, You will be the Compassionate One. If you are the Compassionate One, You will be the Benevolent One. If you are the Benevolent One, You will be the Holy One. without status, what need is there to dissolve the provisional wisdoms of the many? When merit and status are transformed, the essence and function become clear; when right and partiality are both reached, the profound mystery is distinguished.
Who can fathom the killing and enlivening at the point of the blade? The mechanism of the Ultimate cannot be transmitted.
The monk asked again, "Why did Linji establish these Three Mysteries and Three Essentials?

The Master said, "It was also like urinating on one's own bed with one's eyes open. The monk pressed further, "What of those who realize the meaning of these mysteries and essentials? The Master said:
"Where is the 'hair-cutting sword'? He also indicated this with a verse: "Having received the blow, what need is there for mystery?

Offerings. In my decrepit old age, how can I bear to clasp my hands once more?
Having departed from Dongyuan, I have returned to hide away at Wuyi for ten years;
yet my secluded dreams remain unfulfilled. With a single heart of cold resolve, I swear my vow alone. Let out a few long sighs as I return home.
Thus it is. Sixty-six wondrous peaks arise from the tip of the staff.
Master Sheng fled from Shouchang because of old ties;
he comes and goes, disappearing from head to tail. This fellow is a white-handed thief who has all his life been accustomed to the edge of the blade.
"Acting thus, life and nature are but a hair's breadth—whom can recognize this?
Master Cheng entrusted me with these words: 'There is medicine that will leave behind poison;
the phrase of Bodhidharma conceals a malevolent intent and ultimately poisons oneself. Now, where can one find that Liuzhi? Wind and waves on level ground arise only from within."
Surging! Who can break the waves atop the reeds?
Sent to show you, Fahai, son of the Yellow Rock:

He said: "Do not let these people waste their time in vain.

The thirty-six peaks have no peers; towering and majestic, the tigers roar in solitary loftiness and mystery. The spiritual remains of the former master still abide here;
O son of the Master of the Cave, you may let them go as you please.
Reclining on my horse-pillow at the Azure Bamboo Ridge, I chant idly:
"I have no old friends to reminisce with; though there are the ancients, even reminiscing about them is idle.
It is better to take up my hoe and plant bamboo, watching its lush waves brush against my weathered face."
A new chamber has been constructed at Shiping Rock;
throughout my life, I have never known the tortoise to hide its six limbs. By chance, my body now wanders like wood or stone;
like a drifting cloud, it has no place of abiding, yet today it once again hangs upon the head of the green mountain.
How profound is my decline that I no longer sigh; "Go back, my little ones," for who would linger?
Before the peak, there is joy in the presence of the crescent moon, sufficient to let its pure light be gazed upon for ten thousand ages.
The Layman Youlong, accompanied by several friends, came to visit Boshan yesterday.
What instructions did you give him? Please try to recount them as they were spoken so we may examine them. A smile and silence—would this have been appropriate?
Do not let your tongue deceive you regarding the moment before the pivot of action.
Showing Zhou’s younger brother:
if parents are not kin, who then is kin? If they cannot wait for one another, what kind of people are they? As he was about to pose his question to me, I shouted at the sound;
he suddenly tumbled over, quickly turning himself around.
Showing the Way and inviting inquiry: the Host is clearly you yourself;
why do you go to others to seek him? Fire is the lamp—why did you not realize this sooner? When blown out and extinguished, what then?
At midnight at Longtan, it is difficult to report the dawn.
I met with the Chancellor Ye of Taishan in Futang;
in the past, he personally composed this "Discourse on Deliberation. Meeting by chance today, we share a moment of laughter. Who would willingly acknowledge the radiant pearl atop his topknot?
Wanling has shed its hidden luster for a thousand ages.

our brows were already unfurled with joy. We struck the boat’s railing, once again harmonizing with the poems of Yinpingshan;
atop Listening-Spring Pavilion, we engaged in repeated chanting, which proved too distracting for the single game of chess at Fushan.
Accompanying Chengzi, we stayed at the Phoenix Pavilion. There was a portrait of Great Master Zhenjue by the ancient banyan tree in the city;
looking up and down, I thought only of Old Xuefeng: "Who can understand how to play with those three wooden balls?
How strange is that old fisherman on his boat!"
Visiting Bophae-ssa Temple on Namsan Mountain, I was moved to reflect:
I constantly cherish the memory of the old Master Namsan of yore; How truly marvelous he was, holding fast at the crag’s edge!
Refusing to yield to either of the two masters as they encountered him like tigers— Who could have pierced the red sun with his arrow?
Ascending Mount Wushan at the Old Monastery, who was it that knocked on the door those years ago? Xuefeng pressed him in until he nearly forgot his very soul.
Meeting him now at Wangzhou Pavilion—how many seekers of Chan have here sought refuge and followed in his footsteps?
Wandering at the Pingyuan Terrace, I address the Sangha of the Zhití:
"At the mouth of the Five Hundred Celestial Crowns, a single blow upon the head admits no sentiment. Who has ever seen the ox tracks on Mount Tiantai?

what can be done about Baizhang’s refined style?"
In Zhicheng, I have long shared a spiritual communion with the two lay practitioners Zhang Cunsan and Ke Binming at Jinguantang.

yet now, Yang and Li occupy the vanguard.

Dai Jin: "Now that Inspector Liang has paid a visit, do not conceal from me your dream of flowers before the courtyard. For what reason does the Spirit Mountain gaze with a smile? A single melody fills the mountain moon at dawn;

do not doubt that the person of today is the same as the person of antiquity. When the mind is in constant communion with the sages, this is what constitutes spirit. Su Dongpo could not have grown hair or horns;

Staying at Huixinyuan in Zhapu, the two lay practitioners Zhang Cunsan and Huang Xinjing visited me.

Reuniting again with an old friend, I recognize Master Shiyuan atop Mengbi Xianting Mountain;

Wuzhu and Mañjuśrī discourse in vain; The borrowed melody of the rooster’s cry cannot deceive me. I refuse to let it remain in a state of muddled confusion.
